title: Machine Learning-Based Characterisation of the Non-Markovian Dynamics of a Nitrogen-Vacancy Centre
authors: Tom Lannon, Mauro Paternostro, John Martin Gregg, Amit Kumar
abstract: The interaction between a quantum system and its environment can be characterized by the spectral density function: knowing its structure is important for optimizing applications of quantum technologies such as quantum sensing protocols. In this work, we present the first experimental demonstration of a machine learning-based reconstruction of reaction-coordinate spectral density parameters from NV centre Rabi dynamics. Unlike the previous work, we recover all spectral density parameters rather than only the central frequency, and benchmark the performance of the neural network against the Cramér-Rao bound and maximum likelihood estimator. Our results demonstrate that the model predicted by the neural network can reliably reproduce the NV dynamics over the estimation window, and can produce estimates for some parameters with variances comparable to that of maximum likelihood.
summary: This paper reports the first experimental use of machine learning to reconstruct the full spectral density parameters governing the non-Markovian dynamics of an NV center. By analyzing Rabi oscillations from ODMR measurements, the authors trained a neural network to estimate environmental parameters, showing performance comparable to established quantum estimation techniques.
main_problem: The primary goal is to characterize the non-Markovian dynamics of a quantum system, specifically an NV center, by reconstructing the spectral density function parameters from experimental Rabi dynamics.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that a machine learning approach can reconstruct all spectral density parameters from the NV dynamics, achieving variance estimates comparable to the Maximum Likelihood Estimator for certain parameters.
method: The study combines experimental measurements (ODMR/Rabi oscillations) with advanced computational techniques, using neural networks trained to map measured dynamics onto underlying environmental spectral density parameters.
model_or_system: The system is a negatively charged Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) center in diamond, modeled as a spin-boson system. Non-Markovian dynamics are incorporated via a Reaction Coordinate (RC) mapping, which governs the system's interaction with its environment.
key_observables:
Pulsed ODMR signal, Rabi oscillations ($\langle\sigma_z(t)angle$), and the reconstructed spectral density parameters ($\gamma, 
u, \lambda, T$).
important_parameters:
The spectral density parameters ($\gamma, 
u, \lambda, T$) characterizing the environment's coupling to the quantum system.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the RC mapping to handle strong coupling and non-Markovian effects, and the ML approach is benchmarked against the Cramér-Rao bound and MLE.

paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical model (NV center, spin-boson), details the experimental measurements (ODMR/Rabi), presents the ML methodology for parameter estimation, compares its performance against theoretical bounds (CRB/MLE), and concludes with a proposed two-step estimation workflow.
why_interesting: This work represents a powerful synergy between quantum physics and AI, showing how ML can extract detailed spectral information about open quantum systems that is otherwise difficult to measure or model accurately.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A schematic of the machine-learning based parameter estimation procedure. A continuous microwave signal drives the spin of the NV centre between two states, resulting in a photoluminescence signal that oscillates and decays (possibly non-monotonically) in time due to coupling to an external environment. This signal is fed into a trained neural network to perform regression on the parameters of the environment. These parameters are used to simulate a reaction coordinate model of the NV dynamics that is able to reproduce the experimental data.

Figure 2. ODMR signal in the ground state of the NV centre. Green points are experimental data, and the black line is a fit to the fine structure Hamiltonian. The relevant energy levels and transitions for this experiment are shown in the inset.

Figure 3. Normalised pulsed ODMR signal in the electronic transition |0⟩→|+1⟩of the NV centre. Green points are experimental data, and the black line is a fit to the hyperfine Hamiltonian. The relevant energy levels and transitions for this experiment are shown in the inset, and the orange dashed line indicates the transition that is addressed during Rabi oscillation experiments.

Figure 4. NV centre Rabi oscillations. The green points are experimental data normalised between the PL of the |0⟩state and the PL after the first π-pulse. The solid blue (orange) line is the RC model with parameters returned by the neural net- work trained on simulated data of duration 7.5 µs (10 µs). The vertical dashed lines indicate the duration of experimental data fed into the corresponding neural network.

Figure 5. The time derivative of the trace distance between initial states |0⟩and |1⟩under the map corresponding to the predicted RC model. Regions above the horizontal dashed line indicate a backflow of information.
